> **How to read this file.** Section 3 runs the simulation, sections 4 and 5 show the evidence, and section 8 states my selected n. The reusable code lives in `R/functions.R`; this file only calls it.

## 1. Prediction

The Exponential is strongly right-skewed: lots of small values and a long tail of big ones. I predict that skewness is what holds it back, and that it needs far more observations than the die. I guess the selected n will be somewhere around 70 to 75.

## 2. The population

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("R/setup.R")
source("R/functions.R")

generator <- function(n) rexp(n, rate = 1)
mu    <- 1
sigma <- 1
```

Exponential with rate λ = 1: mean μ = 1/λ = `r mu`, standard deviation σ = 1/λ = `r sigma`, so the theoretical standard error of the mean is σ/√n = 1/√n.

Its shape is very skewed: skewness 2 and excess kurtosis 6. For an average of n independent observations these shrink to **2/√n** and **6/n**, so I can compare my simulation with that theory.

```{r}
#| label: population-plot
#| fig-height: 3
curve(dexp(x, rate = 1), from = 0, to = 6, lwd = 3, col = "steelblue",
      main = "Exponential(1) population", xlab = "x", ylab = "density")
```

## 3. Simulation

For every sample size n in my list (`r min(n_values)` to `r max(n_values)`, `r length(n_values)` sizes), I draw B = `r format(B, big.mark = ",")` samples of n observations and keep each sample's mean. B is the number of repetitions; n is the size of each sample.

```{r}
#| label: simulate
all_means <- simulate_all_n(generator, n_values)
results   <- summarize_means(all_means, mu, sigma)
results$good <- flag_good(results)
n_star <- smallest_good_n(results)

dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
write.csv(results, "results/03_exponential.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

## 4. Results

Selected sample sizes (the full table of all `r nrow(results)` sizes is saved in `results/03_exponential.csv`). The columns `theory_skew` and `theory_kurtosis` are 2/√n and 6/n:

```{r}
#| label: table
key_n <- sort(unique(c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 75, 100, n_star)))
show  <- results[results$n %in% key_n, c("n", "sim_mean", "theory_mean", "sim_sd",
                                         "theory_se", "sd_ratio", "skewness",
                                         "excess_kurtosis")]
show$theory_skew     <- 2 / sqrt(show$n)
show$theory_kurtosis <- 6 / show$n
show$passes <- ifelse(results$good[results$n %in% key_n], "yes", "no")
knitr::kable(show, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

## 5. Plots

**Histograms of the sample means**, with the theoretical normal curve N(μ, σ/√n) in red. I show the same sample sizes in every analysis (1, 2, 5, 30) plus my selected n:

```{r}
#| label: histograms
show_n <- sort(unique(c(1, 2, 5, 30, n_star)))
plot_histograms(all_means, show_n, mu, sigma, "Exponential(1)")
```

**Q–Q plots** (points on the red line = normal):

```{r}
#| label: qqplots
plot_qq(all_means, show_n, "Exponential(1)")
```

These sample sizes are a sample of the picture: 1 is the raw population, 2 is the smallest amount of averaging, 5 is a small sample, 30 is the classic rule of thumb, and the last one is my selected n. Every n from 1 to 100 appears in the diagnostics chart below and in `results/03_exponential.csv`, and you can see the sampling distribution at any n in the [Interactive Sampling Distribution Explorer](https://nprodhuturi.github.io/clt-monte-carlo/interactive/explorer.html).

**Diagnostics across every n.** Dashed lines mark my "approximately normal" limits (defined in section 6). The blue lines are the theory, 2/√n for skewness and 6/n for kurtosis:

```{r}
#| label: diagnostics
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(results$n, results$skewness, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.6,
     ylim = range(c(results$skewness, -0.25, 0.25)),
     xlab = "n", ylab = "skewness", main = "Skewness of sample means")
abline(h = c(-0.25, 0, 0.25), lty = c(2, 1, 2), col = "firebrick")
lines(results$n, 2 / sqrt(results$n), col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)

plot(results$n, results$excess_kurtosis, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.6,
     ylim = range(c(results$excess_kurtosis, -0.5, 0.5)),
     xlab = "n", ylab = "excess kurtosis", main = "Excess kurtosis")
abline(h = c(-0.5, 0, 0.5), lty = c(2, 1, 2), col = "firebrick")
lines(results$n, 6 / results$n, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)

plot(results$n, results$sd_ratio, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.6,
     ylim = range(c(results$sd_ratio, 0.95, 1.05)),
     xlab = "n", ylab = "simulated SD / theoretical SE", main = "Spread vs. theory")
abline(h = c(0.95, 1, 1.05), lty = c(2, 1, 2), col = "firebrick")
```

## 6. My definition of "approximately normal"

I use the same rule in every analysis. A sample size n counts as approximately normal when **all four** of these hold:

1.  The histogram is bell-shaped and the Q–Q plot is close to the line.
2.  \|skewness\| ≤ 0.25.
3.  \|excess kurtosis\| ≤ 0.5.
4.  The simulated SD is within 5% of the theoretical SE (σ/√n).

My selected n is the smallest n that passes and stays passing for every larger n I tested, so a lucky pass at one n doesn't count. The reasons for each cutoff are in [01_standard_normal.md](01_standard_normal.md).

## 7. Interpretation

```{r}
#| label: interpretation
at_star  <- results[results$n == n_star, ]
before   <- results[results$n < n_star, ]
below    <- before[nrow(before), ]
at_one   <- results[results$n == 1, ]
sd_lo    <- min(results$sd_ratio)
sd_hi    <- max(results$sd_ratio)
max_mean_err <- max(abs(results$sim_mean - results$theory_mean))
skew_gap <- max(abs(results$skewness - 2 / sqrt(results$n)))
n_theory <- ceiling((2 / 0.25)^2)
```

- **Shape.** At n = 1 the histogram is the Exponential itself: a tall spike near 0 and a long right tail, and the Q–Q plot bends sharply away from the line. As n grows the pile of sample means becomes less lopsided, and by n = 30 it is bell-like but still has a slightly longer right tail.
- **Mean.** The simulated mean never differs from μ = 1 by more than `r round(max_mean_err, 3)`. Averaging doesn't change the center.
- **Spread.** The simulated SD divided by the theoretical SE stays between `r round(sd_lo, 3)` and `r round(sd_hi, 3)`, so σ/√n holds at every n.
- **Skewness decides it.** At n = 1 the skewness is `r round(at_one$skewness, 3)` (theory 2). It falls like 2/√n, and my simulation follows that curve (largest gap `r round(skew_gap, 3)`). The kurtosis falls like 6/n, which is much faster, so it is never the problem here.
- **Theory check.** Setting 2/√n = 0.25 gives n = (2/0.25)² = `r n_theory`. My list of sample sizes only has 45, 50, 75 and 100 above 40, so the first size I tested that is at or past that point and stays passing is n = `r n_star`.

**CLT assumptions.** The observations are independent and identically distributed with finite variance, so every assumption is met. The CLT is true here; it is just slow because of the skew.

**Limitations / surprises.** The surprise is how far the classic n = 30 is from the finish line: at n = 30 the skewness is still about `r round(results$skewness[results$n == 30], 2)`, above my 0.25 limit. Also, the passing point depends on my cutoff. Near the limit the simulated skewness only changes slowly with n, and random noise of about ±`r round(sqrt(6 / B), 2)` can move the point where it first stays under 0.25, so I treat n = `r n_star` as a rough answer and not an exact one.

## 8. Selected n and justification

| **Final answer: n = `r n_star`** |
|:--------------------------------:|

$$\boxed{n = `r n_star`}$$

**Evidence at n = `r n_star`.** Skewness `r round(at_star$skewness, 3)` (limit ±0.25), excess kurtosis `r round(at_star$excess_kurtosis, 3)` (limit ±0.5), and SD ratio `r round(at_star$sd_ratio, 3)` (limit 1 ± 0.05). The histogram follows the normal curve closely, and the Q–Q plot follows the line.

- **Why not smaller.** At n = `r below$n`, the skewness is `r round(below$skewness, 3)`, which is outside my ±0.25 limit (the theory says it should be about `r round(2 / sqrt(below$n), 3)`).
- **It stays passing.** Every larger n I tested, up to n = `r max(n_values)`, also passes.
- **Is the number 30?** No. For the Exponential, 30 is too small: at n = 30 the skewness is still about `r round(results$skewness[results$n == 30], 2)`. By the theory I need about n = `r n_theory`, so 30 is roughly `r round(n_star / 30, 1)` times too small.
